title: Introducing BioseqDB
text:
BioseqDB is a PostgreSQL extension for storing, indexing and searching biological sequences with SQL.

I wanted to keep sequences and their metadata together. An organism, collection date or patient identifier can be an ordinary column beside its DNA, and sequence alignment can sit in the same query as a filter or join.

The introduction has two small SQL examples, the history of the project, a comparison with existing aligners and a Docker quick start. This first release is experimental software; I would like to hear how it works with your data.

Read on BioseqDB: https://bioseqdb.com/blog/introducing-bioseqdb/

title: Combining search results in PostgreSQL
text:
A search can lose the right row before ranking has even finished.

In this small PostgreSQL experiment, applying LIMIT before a study filter leaves only one result when two eligible notes exist. Then I combine text and vector candidate lists with reciprocal rank fusion, without adding scores that mean different things.

The examples use invented distances and ranks, so you can inspect each decision in ordinary SQL without an embedding model. The useful distinction is which rows enter the answer, then how to order them.

title: What does vector mean in PostgreSQL?
text:
What does “vector” mean in PostgreSQL?

A tsvector contains searchable terms. An embedding contains coordinates from a chosen representation. An array can hold measurements, while vectorized execution describes how a database processes batches of values.

Those are different jobs, even when they share a word. This post follows one specimen record through small SQL examples, including why the same <-> operator can mean different things for different operand types.

Read on BioseqDB: https://bioseqdb.com/blog/what-does-vector-mean-in-postgres/

title: Full-text search rules I can explain in SQL
text:
I find search easier to work on when I can point at a row and explain why it belongs in the result.

This example starts with a small rule: find a specimen note containing the phrase “low coverage”, or both “repeat” and “extraction”. The query returns the matching reason beside each row.

From there, the post builds a stored tsvector document, adds a GIN index and shows how the Rails pg_search gem can use that column. The gem and the separate PostgreSQL extension named pg_search are different projects; this example uses the gem.

Read on BioseqDB: https://bioseqdb.com/blog/full-text-search-rules-in-sql/

title: Where PostgreSQL table storage can change
text:
Choosing a B-tree index does not turn a PostgreSQL table into a B-tree table.

A table access method owns the table's rows; an index access method helps locate candidates. The SQL examples in this post inspect both through pg_am and pg_class, then follow the boundary into scans, snapshots and tuple callbacks.

Returning the first row is only the beginning of a storage experiment. Updates, overlapping readers, VACUUM and recovery still need answers. This is the SQL-side introduction to the longer C++ table access method tutorial.

Read on BioseqDB: https://bioseqdb.com/blog/where-postgres-table-storage-can-change/

title: Comparing butterfly genomes with BioseqDB, SQLAlchemy and Plotly
text:
What happens if we put butterfly DNA into PostgreSQL?

I wrote a tutorial comparing two Heliconius species around optix, a gene involved in their red wing patterns. We import a one-million-base region from each species, count A/C/G/T, measure GC content and find matching stretches of DNA.

The sequences come from NCBI through SQL. BioseqDB stores and aligns them inside PostgreSQL; SQLAlchemy sends the queries, and Plotly draws the results. No separate alignment executable is needed.

We start with one match, draw all the retained alignments, then zoom in on optix with gene annotations and local GC measurements. There are a few useful gotchas along the way, from coordinate conventions to reverse-complement matches. Similar GC percentages certainly don't mean the sequences are the same!

The complete Python code, SQL and notebook are available in the examples repository linked from the article.

One setup detail: the current 0.1.0-alpha.1 Docker images and native packages omit the NCBI integration. For this tutorial, build from source with BIOSEQ_BUILD_EXTERNAL_API_CLIENTS=ON; the article explains how.

Read on BioseqDB: https://bioseqdb.com/blog/comparing-butterfly-genomes-with-bioseqdb/
Read on Medium: https://medium.com/@styczynski/comparing-butterfly-genomes-with-bioseqdb-sqlalchemy-and-plotly-62dda57c6d9b
